interactions.label: A 3-year-old child presents with fever, cough, and crepitations in the right low

params.question: A 3-year-old child presents with fever, cough, and crepitations in the right lower zone. He is feeding well, maintaining normal oxygen saturation, and will be treated with oral amoxicillin as an outpatient. What is the most appropriate imaging decision?

answers.text: Order a frontal and lateral chest radiograph to confirm the diagnosis before starting antibiotics

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Routine chest radiography — including a lateral view — is not required for uncomplicated community-acquired pneumonia in children. The WHO and most guidelines state the diagnosis is clinical when the child is stable.

answers.text: Perform a chest ultrasound to exclude pleural effusion before discharge

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Chest ultrasound is indicated when a pleural opacity is seen on radiograph or clinical signs suggest effusion (dull, silent lung base). In this uncomplicated case with no such signs, it is not warranted.

answers.text: No chest radiograph is required, as the diagnosis is clinical and the case is uncomplicated

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The WHO explicitly states that routine radiography is not required to diagnose or manage uncomplicated pneumonia. This child is clinically stable, feeding well, and not hypoxic — imaging would not change the treatment plan.

answers.text: Order a frontal chest radiograph only if the child does not improve within 24 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The threshold for imaging is 48–72 hours of non-response to appropriate antibiotics, not 24 hours. Even then, imaging is prompted by clinical deterioration or suspicion of a complication such as effusion.

overallFeedback.feedback: The WHO explicitly states that routine chest radiography is not required for uncomplicated pneumonia in children. This child is feeding well and not hypoxic — the diagnosis is clinical, and imaging would add radiation without changing the management plan.

Well done. The WHO recommends against routine chest radiography in uncomplicated community-acquired pneumonia in children. Children are especially radiosensitive, and imaging should be reserved for cases where it would change management.

interactions.label: A 4-year-old child with pneumonia has persistent fever despite 72 hours of appro

params.question: A 4-year-old child with pneumonia has persistent fever despite 72 hours of appropriate antibiotics. The chest radiograph shows a pleural opacity at the right lung base. Which investigation should be performed next?

answers.text: CT thorax with contrast to characterise the pleural fluid

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CT is reserved for complications such as necrotising pneumonia or lung abscess. Ultrasound is the appropriate next step for pleural fluid — it carries no ionising radiation and directly characterises the fluid.

answers.text: Chest ultrasound to distinguish simple effusion from septated empyema

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Ultrasound carries no ionising radiation and is more sensitive than the plain film for small effusions. Crucially, it distinguishes a simple, free-flowing effusion from a septated, loculated empyema and guides the drainage site.

answers.text: Lateral chest radiograph for better visualisation of the pleural space

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A lateral radiograph adds radiation dose without significant diagnostic benefit in this context. Ultrasound is the investigation of choice for characterising pleural fluid in children.

answers.text: Repeat frontal chest radiograph in 48 hours to assess progression

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: With persistent fever at 72 hours and a visible pleural opacity, further characterisation of the fluid is needed now — not passive observation. The child needs ultrasound to determine whether drainage is required.

overallFeedback.feedback: When a pleural opacity is seen on the chest radiograph, ultrasound is the next step — not CT or a repeat film. It carries no ionising radiation, is more sensitive for small effusions, and can distinguish free-flowing fluid from septated empyema, directly guiding the decision to drain.

Correct. When a pleural opacity is visible on the chest radiograph, the clinical pearl is: reach for the probe, not the scanner. Ultrasound carries no radiation, is more sensitive than the plain film, and distinguishes simple effusion from septated empyema.

interactions.label: On the expiratory chest radiograph of a toddler with a witnessed choking episode

params.question: On the expiratory chest radiograph of a toddler with a witnessed choking episode, the left lung appears hyperinflated while the right lung has deflated normally. The mediastinum has shifted to the right. Which of the following best explains this pattern?

answers.text: Partial obstruction of the left main bronchus acting as a ball-valve, trapping air on expiration

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Partial bronchial obstruction acts as a ball-valve — air enters during inspiration but cannot escape during expiration. The obstructed left lung remains hyperinflated, and the increased pressure shifts the mediastinum away from the affected side (to the right).

answers.text: Complete obstruction of the left main bronchus causing distal collapse

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Complete obstruction causes collapse, not hyperinflation. The affected lung would be opacified and the mediastinum would shift toward (not away from) the obstructed side.

answers.text: Complete obstruction of the right main bronchus causing right-sided collapse

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: If the right bronchus were completely obstructed, the right lung would appear collapsed and opacified, not normally deflated. The clinical finding here — left hyperinflation with rightward mediastinal shift — points to left-sided air trapping.

answers.text: A left-sided tension pneumothorax displacing the mediastinum

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While tension pneumothorax also causes contralateral mediastinal shift, the clinical context of a choking episode and the finding of hyperinflation (not absent lung markings) indicate air trapping from foreign body aspiration, not pneumothorax.

overallFeedback.feedback: In partial bronchial obstruction, a ball-valve mechanism traps air in the affected lung. On expiration, the obstructed side stays hyperinflated while the normal side deflates. The mediastinum shifts away from the hyperinflated (obstructed) side. The key rule: air trapping pushes away, collapse pulls toward.

Excellent. Partial bronchial obstruction creates a ball-valve mechanism — air enters the obstructed lung on inspiration but is trapped on expiration. The hyperinflated lung pushes the mediastinum away from the affected side. Remember: air trapping pushes away, collapse pulls toward.

interactions.label: A 9-month-old infant with a febrile urinary tract infection has a normal renal u

params.question: A 9-month-old infant with a febrile urinary tract infection has a normal renal ultrasound. What is the significance of this normal result?

answers.text: It excludes vesicoureteric reflux, confirming that no further imaging is needed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ultrasound shows structure — hydronephrosis, size asymmetry, cortical thinning — but it cannot detect vesicoureteric reflux. Reflux can be present even with a completely normal ultrasound.

answers.text: It indicates that DMSA scintigraphy is unnecessary since cortical damage would have been visible on ultrasound

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ultrasound may show cortical thinning as a surrogate for scarring, but subtle cortical damage is better detected by DMSA scintigraphy, which reveals photopenic defects where tracer uptake is reduced.

answers.text: It confirms normal anatomy but cannot exclude reflux or subtle cortical damage — further imaging may still be indicated based on the risk profile

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A normal ultrasound confirms normal renal anatomy but does not exclude reflux or subtle cortical damage. In a young infant with a febrile UTI, further investigation with MCUG (to detect and grade reflux) and/or DMSA (to assess for cortical scarring) may still be indicated.

answers.text: It means the infection was confined to the lower tract, so antibiotic prophylaxis is not required

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The site of infection (upper vs lower tract) is determined clinically by the presence of fever, not by ultrasound findings. A normal ultrasound does not reclassify a febrile UTI as a lower-tract infection.

overallFeedback.feedback: A normal ultrasound shows normal structure but cannot exclude reflux or subtle cortical damage. In a young infant with a febrile UTI, further imaging with MCUG and/or DMSA may still be indicated — each tool answers a different clinical question.

Correct. A normal renal ultrasound confirms normal anatomy but has important blind spots — it cannot detect vesicoureteric reflux or subtle cortical damage. That is exactly why the MCUG and DMSA scan exist as complementary investigations.

interactions.label: Which principle should guide the choice of imaging modality across all three pae

params.question: Which principle should guide the choice of imaging modality across all three paediatric conditions discussed — chest infection, foreign body aspiration, and urinary tract infection?

answers.text: Always perform CT imaging first, as it provides the most comprehensive anatomical information

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CT carries the highest radiation dose among routine investigations and is reserved for specific complications. The imaging hierarchy begins with the lowest-dose option — plain radiograph or ultrasound.

answers.text: Use the lowest-dose investigation that answers the specific clinical question, and avoid imaging when it will not change management

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The ALARA principle (As Low As Reasonably Achievable) and Image Gently guidelines require choosing the test that answers the clinical question with the least ionising radiation. If the result will not change what you do, the radiation exposure was never justified.

answers.text: Reserve all imaging until the child fails to respond to 72 hours of empirical treatment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While non-response to antibiotics is one indication for imaging in pneumonia, other conditions follow different logic — foreign body aspiration requires evaluation based on the choking history, and UTI imaging follows age-based risk stratification.

answers.text: Perform all available imaging modalities in sequence to avoid missing any diagnosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Performing all modalities exposes the child to unnecessary radiation. Children are more radiosensitive than adults and have decades for harm to manifest. Each investigation must be justified by a specific clinical question it will answer.

overallFeedback.feedback: The governing rule across all three conditions is the same: use the lowest-dose investigation that answers the clinical question. Children are more radiosensitive than adults, and every imaging order must be justified by its potential to change management.

Correct. The ALARA principle applies across all paediatric imaging — choose the lowest-dose investigation that answers the clinical question. If imaging will not change management, the radiation was not justified.
